headline: Slow a child's growth
body: It's called catch-up growth and it shouldn't be possible if height ran on a clock.
punch: The fact that it happens tells you what height actually runs on.

headline: If growth were a timer
body: Illness, malnutrition, glucocorticoids — anything that suppresses growth for months should cost you those months permanently. It doesn't.
punch: Release the brake and the growth rate exceeds normal for age.

headline: Because suppressing growth
body: Growth plates have a finite number of cell divisions. Slow the division rate and you slow the depletion of that reserve at the same time.
punch: You didn't lose time. You spent the account slower.

headline: This has been tested
body: It isn't specific to one hormone. Hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid excess and other unrelated growth inhibitors all delay growth plate senescence the same way.
punch: Senescence tracks cumulative proliferation, not calendar age.

headline: It even works
body: Infuse a growth inhibitor into one rabbit's tibia and only that plate slows — then only that plate overshoots afterward. The other leg is unaffected.
punch: Which rules out any central or systemic explanation.

headline: But there is a limit
body: Estrogen does two separate things. It suppresses growth rate — fully reversible. And it depletes the progenitor pool structurally — not reversible, still measurable five weeks after treatment stops.
punch: One of those you get back. The other you don't.

headline: Which is the real distinction
body: Slowed growth can be recovered. Spent cells cannot. Two interventions can look identical on a growth chart and leave you in completely different positions.
punch: The chart doesn't show you which one happened.

headline: And catch-up isn't infinite
body: It's well documented after transient suppression. Whether it fully restores predicted adult height depends on duration, severity and timing — and often it doesn't.
punch: Partial recovery is the normal outcome. Not full.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
